title: Iraq's New PM Ali al-Zaidi Sworn In with Partial Cabinet
summary: Iraq's new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi was sworn in on Thursday with only a partial cabinet, after parliament failed to reach consensus on several key posts, including interior and defence. In Iraq, a government wins a confidence vote when parliament approves half plus one of its ministries. Al-Zaidi's government should include 23 ministers, but lawmakers approved only 14 during the session. Negotiations continue over the remaining portfolios. Among the confirmed ministers are Basim Mohammed as oil minister and Fuad Hussein, who retained his post as foreign minister. Al-Zaidi presented his government programme during the session, which was not broadcast live, and has yet to announce it publicly. At 40, al-Zaidi is Iraq's youngest prime minister. He was chosen on April 27 after President Nizar Amedi named him prime minister-designate, breaking a months-long deadlock. The previous frontrunner, former two-time Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, was fiercely opposed by US President Donald Trump, who warned that all support to Iraq would stop if al-Maliki became PM. Al-Zaidi has no history in political office or government administration. Born in Baghdad to a prominent family, he built his career in the private and academic sectors, holding degrees in law and finance and a master's in banking and finance. Analysts say his lack of political history is his greatest asset in a deeply polarized landscape. His "blank slate" makes him a palatable choice domestically and internationally. Al-Zaidi faces major challenges: disarming Iran-backed militias, tackling entrenched corruption, and balancing ties between Washington and Tehran. Whether he can succeed remains to be seen.
why_it_matters: Iraq’s new prime minister faces a country divided by sectarian interests and foreign influence. For a 13-year-old, this shows how a leader without a political record can emerge in a crisis, but also how unstable governments can affect everything from security to economic opportunities in a region that supplies much of the world’s oil.

background_read: Iraq has a parliamentary system where the prime minister must be approved by a majority of the 329-seat legislature. Since the 2003 U.S. invasion, the post has been held by a Shia Arab, while the presidency goes to a Kurd and the speaker to a Sunni Arab.

Nouri al-Maliki, who served as premier from 2006 to 2014, was accused of sectarian policies and corruption and is seen by Washington as too close to Iran. President Trump's warning to cut support effectively blocked his return.
President Nizar Amedi, a Kurdish politician, named al-Zaidi after the main blocs failed to agree on a candidate for months—a deadlock reflecting deep polarization.
Ali al-Zaidi, born in 1984, comes from a family with political ties but built his own career in law, finance, and banking, earning a master's in banking before entering the private sector.
The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella of mostly Shia militias backed by Iran, have been integrated into the state but operate independently, challenging Baghdad's authority.
Iraq ranks among the world's most corrupt countries; al-Zaidi's promise to tackle corruption faces resistance from entrenched networks that span the government.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Iraq’s new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sworn in with only a partial cabinet.
└─ DETAIL: Only 14 of 23 ministers approved; key security posts like interior and defence remain vacant.
MECHANICS: A confidence vote requires half plus one of the ministries to be approved.
KEY APPOINTMENTS: Basim Mohammed (oil), Fuad Hussein (foreign) are confirmed.
POLITICAL JOURNEY: Al-Zaidi, 40, is the youngest PM, named after President Amedi broke a months-long deadlock.
└─ PREVIOUS FRONTRUNNER: Nouri al-Maliki blocked by Trump’s threat to cut support.
PROFILE: No prior political office; background in private sector and academia, degrees in law and finance.
└─ ANALYST VIEW: His lack of history is a ‘blank slate’, making him broadly acceptable.
CHALLENGES AHEAD: Disarming Iran-backed militias, fighting entrenched corruption, and balancing US-Iran relations.
└─ OPEN QUESTION: Whether he can succeed remains to be seen.

perspectives.description: Supporters of al-Zaidi, including many Iraqis exhausted by political infighting, hope his clean record and technocratic background will allow him to push through reforms without being tied to corrupt networks. International players may also give him a chance due to his lack of baggage.

Critics argue that his inexperience is a liability: without political allies or deep knowledge of government, he may be manipulated by established power brokers. The failure to fill defence and interior posts leaves the state vulnerable to militias and security threats.

Iraq’s political system, based on ethno-sectarian power-sharing after 2003, produces deadlocked governments and weak prime ministers. Al-Zaidi’s partial cabinet reflects this structural problem, not just personal challenges, and any leader will struggle against the same entrenched forces.

Looking ahead, al-Zaidi must quickly secure the remaining ministries and prove he can tackle corruption and rein in militias. If he fails, Iraq could face more political paralysis or even renewed conflict, further destabilizing the Middle East.
